title: The Deepfake Money Expert Ad
summary: A sponsored social ad uses a familiar money expert and a tech billionaire to promote a bitcoin platform. A caller says profitable months are coming and asks for fast deposits.

post.body: Sponsored: Martin Lewis and Elon Musk finally reveal a bitcoin platform for ordinary people. Earn extra money before Christmas. Leave your details and an adviser calls back in minutes - profitable months are coming, so invest quickly.
post.mediaCaption: Video: "The banks do not want people to know about this"
post.mediaAlt: Line drawing of a money-expert presenter in a TV studio with pound and bitcoin graphics behind him

comments.name: ClareP
comments.text: My first withdrawal worked instantly. This is the one.

comments.name: MoneyWinNow

comments.name: Aaron
comments.text: Why is this not on Martin Lewis's own site?

comments.name: FastReturns

reactionOptions: I want to ask someone first

stop.message: STOP is especially important when a familiar face appears to remove doubt. Capture your first pull before the ad, comments, or caller turn that feeling into action.

source.message: Who is behind the offer? A recognizable face in a video is not the same as an accountable source.

findings.label: Celebrity endorsement is not on official channels
findings.detail: Martin Lewis has repeatedly warned that scammers use his face in fake investment adverts.

findings.label: Signup link is an unrelated domain
findings.detail: The link is not a verified page for the named expert, the billionaire, or a regulated investment firm.

findings.label: Private caller takes over quickly
findings.detail: The BBC story describes victims being called within minutes and moved into one-on-one pressure.

findings.label: Ad creates a short window
findings.detail: Fast callbacks and claims that profitable months are coming are designed to reduce time for independent checks.

question.prompt: Which source signal should you check first?

options.label: Whether the expert endorsed it on official channels
Whether the link belongs to a real regulated firm
Who the caller really works for
Whether the testimonials are real people

question.insight: A scam can borrow trust from a real person while hiding the true operator. Trace the offer to an official, accountable source before giving details or money.

content.message: Now scan the message itself. What is it trying to make you feel, believe, or do before you verify?

question.prompt: What pressure signals do you see?

options.label: Urgency around profitable months and fast action
Moving from public ad to private phone call
Comments that make success look common

question.insight: The ad does not need you to understand the investment. It needs you to feel trust, hope, and urgency long enough to hand over contact details and deposits.

alignment.message: Real financial opportunities leave a trail you can verify outside the ad and outside the caller's script.

results.headline: Victim lost GBP 76,000 after Martin Lewis deepfake advert
results.snippet: The report describes a fake Facebook advert using Martin Lewis and Elon Musk to promote a non-existent bitcoin investment scheme.

results.headline: Martin Lewis warns he does not do investment adverts
results.snippet: Official guidance says celebrity investment adverts using his name or face should be treated as scams.

results.headline: No verified firm behind this domain
results.snippet: The advertised domain does not connect to an accountable, regulated investment provider.

results.headline: Meta says it is cracking down on celebrity scam ads
results.snippet: The platform announced facial-recognition checks because scammers repeatedly abuse public figures in adverts.

question.prompt: What does the outside evidence suggest?

options.label: The investment offer is independently confirmed
This matches a known celebrity deepfake scam pattern
The real source of the offer is not accountable
More verification is needed before acting

question.insight: When independent checks show warnings, missing official endorsement, and an unaccountable domain, the safest answer is not to click, pay, or keep talking to the caller.

reflect.message: Return to the first feeling the ad created. Did familiarity or urgency change how risky the offer seemed?

nextActions.label: Do not click or submit details
Check official consumer or regulator sources
Warn someone who might trust the advert
Report the advert to the platform

reflect.recommendedOutcome: Do not click. End contact. Verify through official consumer and regulator channels.
reflect.rewardMessage: You separated a trusted face from an untrusted offer. That is the habit.
